title: Occasion: Winchester, September 1819
short: Written on 19 September 1819 after a Sunday walk near Winchester; the last of the great odes.
body: Keats was staying in Winchester. On 21 September (Colvin dates the letter 22 September) he wrote to J. H. Reynolds: 'How beautiful the season is now ... I never lik'd stubble fields so much as now ... Somehow a stubble plain looks warm ... this struck me so much in my sunday's walk that I composed upon it.' The walk was probably along the water-meadows of the Itchen, though the exact field is not known. The ode was published in the 1820 Lamia volume. It is often called the most perfect of the odes.

title: Stanza form
short: Three eleven-line stanzas: the ten-line ode stanza extended by one line, with a couplet before the last line.
body: Keats adds a line to the ten-line stanza of the spring odes: a quatrain (abab) followed by a seven-line unit (in stanza 1, cdedcce) in which the couplet falls on lines 9-10, delaying the close. The extra line gives each stanza a feeling of overflow appropriate to its subject ('o'er-brimm'd'). The stanzas move from morning to evening, early to late autumn, and from touch and taste to sight to sound. Unlike the other odes there is no 'I'.

sources.cite: Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem
Walter Jackson Bate, John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1963), chapters on the 1819 odes

title: mists and mellow fruitfulness
short: The opening apostrophe names autumn by its mists and ripeness; 'mellow' means soft and sweet with ripeness.
body: The poem begins with an address, as in a hymn: autumn is called 'Season' and given attributes. 'Mellow' describes fruit that is soft, sweet and fully ripe (OED), and by extension a mature softness of light and sound. The alliteration of m and f, and the long vowels, slow the line. The poem's whole first stanza is one sentence without a main verb, a series of infinitives ('to load and bless', 'to bend', 'to swell') dependent on 'Conspiring'.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'mellow, adj.'
Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem

title: bosom-friend ... Conspiring
short: Autumn and the sun are intimate friends who plot together to load the trees with fruit.
body: 'Bosom-friend' is an intimate companion. 'Conspiring' keeps its etymological sense of breathing together, as well as the sense of secret plotting, here benign. The 'maturing sun' is both the sun that matures the fruit and the sun that is itself maturing towards the lower light of autumn. Some political readings have noted the word 'conspiring' in the year of radical agitation and government suspicion of conspiracy, though this is a minority interpretation.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'conspire, v.'

Nicholas Roe, John Keats and the Culture of Dissent (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997)

title: thatch-eves
short: The eaves of a thatched cottage, round which the vines grow.
body: 'Eves' is an old spelling of 'eaves', the overhanging lower edge of a roof. The picture is of a cottage with vines trained round its thatched eaves, an English rather than Mediterranean vine. The detail joins the 'moss'd cottage-trees' (old apple trees near the cottage) to place the ode in a domestic, cultivated English landscape rather than in classical myth.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'eaves, n.'
John Barnard, ed., John Keats: The Complete Poems (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1973; 3rd ed. 1988), notes to the poem

title: o'er-brimm'd their clammy cells
short: Summer has filled the honeycomb so full that it overflows; 'clammy' means sticky.
body: The bees are deceived by late flowers into thinking 'warm days will never cease', a gentle irony since the poem knows they will. 'Clammy' (moist and sticky) is precise for honeycomb, and 'o'er-brimm'd' suggests overflow, the stanza's keynote and an effect enacted by the eleventh line. Vendler notes that the stanza's abundance is all process and promise ('to set budding more, / And still more'), with ripeness pressing on excess.

sources.cite: Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'clammy, adj.'

anchor: sitting careless on a granary floor
title: Autumn personified
short: Stanza 2 shows Autumn as a figure engaged in, or resting from, the tasks of harvest.
body: Autumn is seen in four guises: sitting 'careless' (carefree) on a granary floor, asleep on a half-reaped furrow, a gleaner crossing a brook, and a watcher at the cider-press. The figure is never gendered explicitly and is drowsy rather than busy; harvest is suspended at each moment. Critics compare classical images of Ceres and the seasons, and painterly analogues have been proposed, though none is certain.

sources.cite: Ian Jack, Keats and the Mirror of Art (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1967)
Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem
Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats, Longman Annotated English Poets (London: Longman, 1970), headnote and notes to the poem

title: winnowing wind
short: The wind that separates grain from chaff; it gently lifts Autumn's hair.
body: To winnow is to separate the light chaff from the heavier grain by tossing it in a current of air, traditionally on a threshing or granary floor. Autumn sits where winnowing is done, and her hair is 'soft-lifted' by the same wind. The image combines labour and repose: the work is done for her by the air. Its casual ease contrasts with the hard labour harvest actually required, a contrast historicist readers have stressed.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'winnow, v.'
Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats, Longman Annotated English Poets (London: Longman, 1970), headnote and notes to the poem

title: hook; swath
short: The reaping-hook or sickle spares the next band of standing corn and its intertwined flowers.
body: The 'hook' is a reaping-hook or sickle; a 'swath' is the strip of corn cut in one sweep, or the line of standing crop to be cut. The reaper, 'Drows'd with the fume of poppies' (poppies grew among the corn, and their juice is opium), has fallen asleep mid-task, so that the next swath and its 'twined flowers' (bindweed, poppies, cornflowers) are spared. The suspension of the sickle has been read as a reprieve from death.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'swath, n.'

Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem

title: like a gleaner
short: One who gathers the ears left after reaping, steadying a heavy load on the head while crossing a brook.
body: Gleaning, the right of the poor to collect what the reapers left, was a customary right still contested in Keats's England (a famous 1788 judgment had limited it). The figure recalls Ruth, gleaner in the fields of Boaz, whom Keats had used in the Nightingale ode. The perfectly balanced line-break ('keep / Steady') mimics the gleaner's steadiness. Some historicist critics see in the image a glance at the rural poor.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Ruth 1:16-22 and 2:1-23
Nicholas Roe, John Keats and the Culture of Dissent (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997)

title: cyder-press ... last oozings
short: Autumn watches the final slow drops of juice from the apple press, hour after hour.
body: 'Cyder' is an old spelling of cider. The patience of the watcher and the slowness of the 'last oozings' stretch out time at the end of the harvest stanza. The word 'last' introduces the note of ending which the third stanza takes up; the line's long vowels and repeated 'hours by hours' enact the dragging time. Cider-making was a central part of the autumn economy in southern English counties such as Hampshire.

sources.cite: Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem
Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats, Longman Annotated English Poets (London: Longman, 1970), headnote and notes to the poem

anchor: Where are the songs of Spring?
title: Where are the songs of Spring?
short: An 'ubi sunt' question, the classic formula of lament, which the poem immediately sets aside.
body: The question echoes the medieval and classical topos of 'ubi sunt' ('where are they [who were before us]?'), as in Villon's 'Mais ou sont les neiges d'antan?'. Keats raises the lament only to dismiss it: 'Think not of them, thou hast thy music too'. The music of autumn that follows (gnats, lambs, crickets, robin, swallows) is a deliberately humble choir, replacing the nightingale of spring.

sources.cite: Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem
Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats, Longman Annotated English Poets (London: Longman, 1970), headnote and notes to the poem
Francois Villon, 'Ballade des dames du temps jadis' (c. 1461)

title: barr'd clouds bloom the soft-dying day
short: Streaks of cloud at sunset make the dying day flower with colour.
body: 'Barr'd' clouds are those lying in horizontal bars or streaks across the sunset. 'Bloom' is used transitively: the clouds make the day bloom, transferring the language of flowers to light. The day is 'soft-dying', a gentle death. The rosy light on the 'stubble-plains' joins the poem to Keats's letter: the stubble plain looked 'warm', like some pictures. The stanza's sound-world is framed by this visual image of evening.

title: stubble-plains
short: The fields left with cut stalks after harvest, which Keats said looked 'warm' on his Winchester walk.
body: Stubble is the short stalks left in the ground after reaping. In his letter to Reynolds of 21 September 1819 Keats praised the season and said that he had never liked stubble fields so much, 'Aye better than the chilly green of the spring', adding that a stubble plain looks warm 'in the same way that some pictures look warm'. In the same letter he associated autumn with Chatterton, whom he called the purest writer in English. The ode thus grows from an observed landscape.

sources.cite: Sidney Colvin, ed., Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends (1891; PD), Project Gutenberg
Hyder E. Rollins, ed., The Letters of John Keats 1814-1821, 2 vols (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1958)
Wikipedia, 'To Autumn' (survey of composition and criticism, with references)

anchor: wailful choir the small gnats mourn
title: wailful choir ... river sallows
short: The gnats' mourning song among the willows, rising and falling with the wind.
body: 'Wailful' means lamenting; the choir of gnats is the first of the autumn musicians and the most elegiac. 'Sallows' are willows, especially the low-growing kinds by rivers (OED). The swarm is 'borne aloft / Or sinking as the light wind lives or dies', a line that enacts in its rhythm the rise and fall and, in its verbs, the poem's movement between life and death.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'sallow, n.1'
Helen Vendler, The Odes of John Keats (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard UP, 1983), chapter on the poem
Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats, Longman Annotated English Poets (London: Longman, 1970), headnote and notes to the poem

title: hilly bourn
short: Either a boundary or region among hills, or a hill stream; editors differ.
body: 'Bourn' (bourne) has two distinct words behind it: a stream or brook (northern 'burn'), and a boundary or limit (French borne), as in Hamlet's 'undiscover'd country from whose bourn / No traveller returns'. Keats elsewhere uses it of a domain or region. Most editors gloss it here as the hilly boundary or region from which the full-grown lambs bleat; the Hamlet echo would bring a faint suggestion of death's frontier.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'bourn, n.1 and n.2'
Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats, Longman Annotated English Poets (London: Longman, 1970), headnote and notes to the poem
William Shakespeare, Hamlet III.i.79-80

title: red-breast ... garden-croft
short: A croft is a small enclosed field near a house; the robin, a winter singer, whistles from it.
body: A croft is a small piece of enclosed ground, often attached to a cottage. The robin ('red-breast') sings through autumn and winter, so its 'treble soft' looks ahead to the coming season. The list of singers in the last lines moves from the low (crickets in the hedge) to the high (swallows in the sky). The homely compound 'garden-croft' keeps the poem in a small, cultivated English landscape to the end.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'croft, n.'
Miriam Allott, ed., The Poems of John Keats, Longman Annotated English Poets (London: Longman, 1970), headnote and notes to the poem

anchor: gathering swallows twitter in the skies
title: gathering swallows
short: Swallows massing before their autumn migration; the poem ends on preparation for departure.
body: Swallows gather in flocks in September before flying south. The final image is thus one of imminent leaving, but it is presented without lament. Critics have read the ending as an image of finality (Bloom), as an image of renewal in the natural cycle (Bate), or, retrospectively, in the light of Keats's own death seventeen months later. The poem never mentions winter.

title: Politics and history
short: Critics disagree on whether the ode evades or obliquely registers the political tensions of 1819.
body: In 1979 Jerome McGann argued that the ode turns away from the political turmoil of 1819, including the Peterloo Massacre (16 August), and offers an idealised, ahistorical England. Nicholas Roe and others have replied that Keats followed the news closely (Henry Hunt's entry into London in September) and that words like 'conspiring', and the images of gleaning and the granary, carry contemporary charge. Others, such as Paul Fry, reject McGann's position and read the poem as an encounter with death. The debate remains open.

sources.cite: Jerome J. McGann, 'Keats and the Historical Method in Literary Criticism', MLN 94 (1979), 988-1032
Nicholas Roe, John Keats and the Culture of Dissent (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997)
